And then they're also cutting corners, making the product worse, and that kind of reflects on the whole brand of WordPress.
turns.zh: 那么，如果我能回顾一下你遇到的问题，我想再深入探讨一下你与 WP Engine 合作中的问题。首先，他们未经授权就使用了 WordPress 和 WooCommerce 的商标，滥用商标，误导公众。许多人以为 WP Engine 实际上是 Automattic 和 WordPress 官方机构。他们没有为项目做出贡献，只是通过收购的公司赚取大量利润，然后像你描述的那样逐步掏空它。此外，他们还偷工减料，降低产品质量，这也损害了 WordPress 的整体品牌形象。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: That's a great summary, yeah.
turns.zh: 总结得很好，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'm curious just which of those three, or is it something even else that most bothered you about this? What's just like, "This is the thing that's eating me"? If I had to guess, it'd be damaging the legacy potentially of this thing you've worked on for most of your life. Maybe it's that, maybe it's just taking advantage of the community. What's the thing that you think is the root of this, just like, "Just this needs to stop"?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很好奇这三个问题中哪一个最让你感到困扰，或者是否还有其他问题。最让你心痛的是什么？如果让我猜测，可能是因为这可能会损害你一生致力于的项目的声誉。也许是利用社区的漏洞。那么你认为问题的根源是什么？就是“必须停止这种行为”？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Well, I guess the one thing I'd add to your list was as this was happening they were pretending to good faith negotiate. And in fact, at one point the executive, we were talking about her joining Automattic and running WordPress out of Oregon and when she thought... the VP and she going to sell, she was thinking about what was next. So yeah, a lot of this stuff was, I think that duplicitous behavior also kind of forced us to an edge more than even those other things that you mentioned. There's lots of companies that don't contribute back and it's not as big a deal. But yeah, the legal issue was definitely the trademark thing. So what pushed it to the edge? I think just the magnitude of the issue. They would refer to themselves as WordPress Engine in client meetings and other things. They were very cavalier about how they would imply their association with the project.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得你提到的清单里还应该加上一点——在整个事件过程中，他们一直假装在真诚谈判。事实上，有一次那位高管，我们当时谈论她加入Automattic并在俄勒冈州运营WordPress的计划。当她以为……副总裁和她要把公司卖掉时，她开始思考下一步该怎么办。所以，我认为这种欺诈行为比你提到的其他因素更让我们走到了绝境。很多公司不回馈开源项目，这倒不是什么大问题。但这次的法律纠纷确实是商标问题引发的。那么，是什么把事情推到了边缘？我觉得是问题的严重性。他们在客户会议上自称"WordPress Engine"，还很轻率地暗示自己与WordPress项目有关联。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Obviously, as you can tell on socials, a lot of people are just really upset and a lot of people blame you. There's just, like I said, every time you're on a podcast or on Twitter, people are just like, "Matt, what about this? Why this sucks? Why are you doing this?" And I want to go through some of those things, but just not many people go through... I think you were like a hundred percent beloved hero of open source and internet and now you're in this... a lot of people don't like you. Just as a human, just what is that? How do you work through that? How do you deal with that? What's that been like?
turns.zh: 显然，从社交媒体上可以看出，很多人非常不满，很多人都在指责你。我说过，每次你上播客或发推特，人们都会问："马特，这个问题怎么看？为什么这么糟糕？你为什么要这么做？"我想详细解答一下这些问题，但很多人不愿意深入探讨……你曾是开源和互联网领域百分百受欢迎的英雄，现在却深陷困境……很多人不喜欢你。从人性角度讲，你怎么看待这种情况？如何克服这些心理？这段经历是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: If you were kind of inside baseball with WordPress, it's actually a lot of people who have been unhappy with me over the years, and when we introduced something like Gutenberg, people hated it. Actually when we introduced a visual editor, people hated it.
turns.zh: 如果你对WordPress内部情况比较了解，就会知道多年来有很多不满我的人。当我们推出Gutenberg时，人们讨厌它。实际上，我们推出可视化编辑器时，人们也反感它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've had practice.
turns.zh: 你对此早有经验了。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: These are huge controversies in the WordPress history. There actually hasn't been a fork or WordPress around all this latest stuff, but there was when we introduced Gutenberg. It's one called ClassicPress where people actually forked the software. So how I would describe it is previously like 1% of the world thought I was terrible, and now I feel like it's up to like 4 or 5%. So it's still not the majority, but as you know, something negative you feel seven times more than something positive. And when people are angry with you, it's kind of like restaurant reviews or whatever, they're more likely to leave a bad review than a good review. (00:53:14): The people who WordPress, 98% of all the core developers have stayed and contribute and are working on the next version and are supportive and all these sorts of things. And part of the reason these folks are so good is they don't spend all their time on Twitter and Reddit arguing with folks, and also the arguments could be... they're very frustrating because people don't engage in good faith. They don't really change their mind when new facts are introduced. (00:53:43): And so I've done my best actually because from the open source side I'm really used to engaging with things, and I think that's been one thing I've learned from this is in some forums it doesn't matter how you engage and especially if you have bots or other things running there. I'd leave comments on Reddit and immediately get like 40 downvotes. I'm like, "Hey, this is a article about me and I'm adding a fact to the thing. Why is it getting downvoted? This is very relevant to the discussion." But it's literally hidden. So when you see that thread, you'd have to click like three or four times to see the comment I had left, and so it can really change the perception. And then when you read these things, I think it's just very human nature. Even folks very close to me, if you read a thread and it's all super negative, it's hard to not be influenced by that because we're social creatures.
turns.zh: 这些在WordPress历史上都是巨大的争议。实际上，关于最近这些事件，WordPress并未分裂成不同分支，但在我们推出Gutenberg时曾出现过分裂。其中一个名为ClassicPress的分支，人们直接分叉了原始软件。用我自己的话说，之前只有1%的人觉得我很糟糕，现在我感觉比例可能上升到了4%或5%。这仍然不是多数，但众所周知，负面情绪比正面情绪更容易被放大。当人们对你生气时，就像餐厅评论之类的，他们更可能留下差评而不是好评。（00:53:14）：WordPress社区的98%核心开发者一直留在项目中，参与开发下一版本，并给予支持。这些人如此优秀的部分原因在于，他们不会把所有时间花在Twitter和Reddit上与人争执，而且争执往往令人沮丧，因为人们不会真诚地参与讨论，当新事实出现时他们也不会改变主意。（00:53:43）：所以我尽了最大努力，因为在开源领域，我习惯于积极参与讨论。我从中学到的一点是，在某些论坛上，无论你如何参与讨论都无关紧要，尤其是如果那里有机器人或其他干扰因素。我在Reddit上留言，立即收到40个踩。当时我说：“嘿，这篇文章是关于我的，我在补充事实。为什么会被踩？这和讨论非常相关。”但评论被隐藏了。所以当你看到那个帖子时，必须点击三四次才能看到我留的评论，这真的会改变人们的看法。然后当你读到这些东西时，我认为这完全是人性使然。即使是和我非常亲近的人，如果你读到一个全是负面评价的帖子，也很难不受其影响，因为我们是社会性动物。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Now the good news is I've had lots of credibility weighted support from people like Marc Benioff or other open source leaders or the core people in WordPress, Matias, Mary Hubbard, all the core committers. The international community actually, like just in Japan, they don't care about this stuff. So these are actually, if you look by number of commits and lines of code and everything like that, the folks who actually are most crucial in WordPress. So I feel like that's been a good balance as well for me because there are days where I'm like, "Gosh, am I an idiot?" or it could be really down reading all these things. So that is part of what allows me to balance and get back to that sort of positive, optimistic space that I think you need to be in to do great software and great work.
turns.zh: 好消息是，我得到了马克·贝尼奥夫等人以及WordPress核心团队成员（如马蒂亚斯、玛丽·哈伯德等所有核心贡献者）的可靠支持。国际社区实际上并不在乎这些事情。就日本而言，他们根本不在乎这些。所以从提交的代码量和行数等指标来看，这些人实际上是WordPress中最关键的角色。所以我觉得这对我来说也是一个很好的平衡，因为有时候我会想：“天哪，我是个白痴吗？”或者读到这些东西时会情绪低落。所以这也是让我保持平衡、回归到那种积极、乐观心态的部分，而我认为你需要保持这种心态才能开发出优秀的软件和完成出色的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The internet can be brutal. Let me go through a couple of specific things that people pointed out because I think you've been on a lot of podcasts and people haven't asked you these questions and I think a lot of people are just like, "But, Matt, what about this? This is really bad." So let me just ask you a couple of things here. One is there's just like a frustration in the community around the instability that this has just caused in the WordPress community. I'll read you a couple quotes. "Real people are receiving fewer projects on WordPress because C-suite are seeing WordPress as unstable because of this feud, and I work at Enterprise and we're very concerned about the stability of this platform and our projects." Just thoughts on that and the impact that it's had on the community.
turns.zh: 是啊，互联网有时确实很无情。让我来谈谈人们提到的几个具体问题，因为我知道你参加了很多播客节目，但人们并没有问到这些问题。我觉得很多人都在想：“但马特，这个问题怎么办？这真的很糟糕。” 所以让我在这里问你几个问题。首先，社区对这场争执给WordPress生态带来的不稳定性感到非常不满。我给你们读几条评论：“因为这场争执，企业高管们认为WordPress不稳定，导致真实用户接到更少的项目。我在企业工作，非常担心这个平台和我们项目的稳定性。” 对此你怎么看？这对社区的影响有多大？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Yeah, I think this is until this gets resolved... which by the way I hope it is soon. I think there's no business reason for this to continue. I really hope that they come to a settlement or something. We're ready. They could end this tomorrow if they wanted to. WP Engine could. We can't. We're just defending right now. So it's really incumbent on them. All of our competitors, by the way, are like, "Great. WordPress, the king on the hill, all of a sudden we can use this." And so there's also not just from WP Engine, but also from all the competitors to WordPress, and all the people who would love to capture some market share, they're really leaning into this. So I've seen white papers, I've seen all sorts of things where people talk about this. (00:56:49): We're actually in the next couple of days going to publish something really cool on the WordPress.org blog though that shows if you actually look at the numbers, like the activity, number of commits, plugin updates, downloads, installs of WordPress since September 20th when this all started, it's quite healthy. And so I'm not saying that there isn't examples of where someone lost a project or something like that. I'm sure it's happened. It's the internet's big. WordPress has so many millions of users and developers and everything that you're going to get some example. But by the numbers things are actually quite healthy, and in some ways it's not that there's no press is bad press, it's raised the awareness of WordPress quite a bit. So people who haven't talked about WordPress in years are now like, "Oh, Let's talk about it." And so a little bit of drama I think, I wouldn't do this all the time, but a little bit can be a good thing.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为在问题解决之前，这种情况会持续下去……顺便说一句，我希望能尽快解决。我觉得这件事没有商业上的必要继续下去。我真的希望他们能达成和解之类的解决方案。我们已经准备好了。如果他们愿意，明天就能结束这一切。WP Engine可以做到，但我们不行。我们现在只能防御。所以这真的取决于他们。顺便说一句，我们所有的竞争对手都在说："太棒了。WordPress这个行业巨头突然成了我们可以利用的机会。" 所以不仅是WP Engine，所有竞争对手，还有那些想抢占市场份额的人，都在大力推动这件事。我看到过各种白皮书，人们都在讨论这个问题。（00:56:49）：事实上，接下来几天我们会在WordPress.org博客上发布一篇很棒的文章。数据显示，自9月20日这场争执开始以来，WordPress的活跃度、提交的代码量、插件更新、下载量和安装量都非常健康。我不是说没有项目丢失之类的情况。我相信这种情况确实发生过。但从数据来看情况其实很乐观。某种程度上，负面新闻未必是坏事，它让更多人关注到了WordPress。那些多年未谈论过WordPress的人现在都在说："哦，让我们聊聊它吧。" 所以我觉得适当的戏剧性冲突也未尝不可，但不能常有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so one of the most common frustrations I've seen on the internet, people complaining is around the trademark. I don't know all the details, but my understanding is there's kind of a... you moved the trademark to be owned by the foundation and Automattic is exclusive rights to use the trademark. And I think people are like, "Oh, I thought it was the foundation owned it, but maybe Matt still owns it and then you're trying to monetize it through this agreement with WP Engine." Is there anything you can share there that'll make people feel and see your side of the story?
turns.zh: 好的，我在网上看到最常见的抱怨之一是关于商标问题。我不了解所有细节，但据我理解，商标现在归基金会所有，而Automattic拥有独家使用权。我觉得人们会想：“哦，我以为商标归基金会所有，但也许马特仍然拥有它，然后你想通过与WP Engine的协议将其商业化。” 你能否分享一些信息，让人们理解你的立场？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Yeah, this is totally fair because it's complicated, but people are saying this has been private. This has all been very public and documented on the internet from the beginning. So WordPress.org has always been me personally, and I think because it's... part of the reason we started there is . com was not available when we started. So that's why we started on the .org and things like that. But I think people also assume .org means nonprofit or something, and that's sometimes true but it's not always. It's not a requirement of the .org domain. Then when I founded Automattic and when we did register the trademark that actually was registered under Automattic. So it used to be, for the first five years of the project or whatever, that Automattic just owned everything outright. And again, I had investors and the board and that was under the control of that. (00:59:06): Now, as Automattic became more successful I was able to consolidate some voting rights and other things and at least later advocate. Also remember, I was like 21 when all this was happening, so I was not maybe the most savvy about legal stuff or didn't always have the best advice. So later as I learned more, I was like, "Oh, I want to actually take this out of the company and create a nonprofit." And so we ended up creating a nonprofit. Now the rules around 501(3)(C) nonprofits run the IRS are actually very strict. So that's also something as people assume, it's like, oh, doesn't the nonprofit run the software, and we applied for that originally and it was denied by the IRS. (00:59:47): So we actually weren't able to put WordPress.org or the software itself under the nonprofit, but we were able to have sort of an educational purview. So what was eventually approved was sort of running the meetups and other things for WordPress, doing educational stuff. We sponsor a lot of learn to code or running workshops in other countries. We have this cool thing called do_action where we'll do a weekend where we take a bunch of nonprofits and build websites for them and stuff like that. So the nonprofit does a lot of exciting things there and then also negotiated with the investors and everyone at Automattic to actually put the trademark under the foundation. (01:00:31): Now the compromise there was that Automattic at this point is running WordPress.com. So to continue running that, which at the time had already tens of millions of users and everything, it needed a commercial license. And so the compromise is that the foundation would kind of own the trademark and license it out for non-commercial purposes. I had a license to run WordPress.org because obviously I need that. And then Automattic would retain the commercial license and the ability to sub-license that, so to sell that to others. So this was kind of the grand compromise and create this tripartite structure. I was very inspired by the three branches of government. So there's sort of power in each of those that I think sort of checks and balances each side of it which is on purpose.
turns.zh: 是啊，这完全公平，因为这事儿确实复杂。但人们总说这事儿一直是私密的，但从一开始这事儿就公开透明，在网上有完整记录。所以WordPress.org一直由我个人运营，我觉得我们选择.ORG的原因之一是，我们刚开始时.com域名没能注册成功。所以我们就选了.ORG之类的域名。但人们还以为.ORG意味着非营利组织之类的，有时确实如此，但也不总是如此。这不是.ORG域名的强制要求。后来我创立了Automattic公司，我们注册了商标，当时实际上是以Automattic的名义注册的。在项目启动的头五年左右，Automattic直接全权拥有所有资产。当时我有投资者和董事会，他们负责把控一切。（00:59:06）：随着Automattic越来越成功，我得以整合一些投票权等权力，至少后来开始倡导相关事务。别忘了，当时我才21岁，处理法律事务时可能不够精通，得到的建议也不总是最佳的。后来我学到更多知识后，就想把这部分业务从公司剥离出来，成立非营利组织。于是我们最终创立了非营利机构。现在美国国税局对501(c)(3)非营利组织的监管非常严格。所以人们常误以为非营利组织会运营软件，我们最初申请时就被国税局拒绝了。（00:59:47）：所以我们最终没能把WordPress.org或软件本身归入非营利组织，但我们获得了教育相关业务的授权。比如组织WordPress聚会、开展教育活动。我们在海外赞助了很多编程学习活动或工作坊。还有个很棒的项目叫do_action，每年周末我们会为非营利组织搭建网站等。非营利组织通过这些活动做了很多出色的工作。之后，我们与Automattic的投资者和团队协商，将商标权授予基金会。（01:00:31）：当前的折中方案是，Automattic继续运营WordPress.com。当时WordPress.com已有数千万用户，维持其商业运营需要商业许可证。折中方案是基金会拥有商标权，并授权其用于非商业用途。我保留了WordPress.org的运营权，因为这对我至关重要。Automattic则保留商业许可证并可转授权他人使用。这就是三方合作的核心架构。我深受三权分立的启发。每个权力分支都相互制衡，形成有力的平衡机制，这正是我们刻意设计的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay, I get why it's complicated. I get why people would be confused. This makes me think about OpenAI had a really strange structure and that got them in a lot of trouble, and it feels like when you're 21 you're like, "Oh, this makes a lot of sense. What a great concept we've come up here," and then all this complexity just adds to a lot of confusion around what's going on. So thank you for addressing that. Another, there's a kind of related question I've seen a couple of times is just why don't you let that .org be run by a community. Why not just give that up to someone else and not just you that's there?
turns.zh: 哇。好吧，我明白这确实很复杂。我也理解人们为何会感到困惑。这让我想到OpenAI之前的组织架构确实很奇怪，结果给自己招来不少麻烦。感觉21岁时你会想：“哦，这太合理了。我们想出的这个概念真是太棒了”，然后这些复杂性却会导致人们对实际情况产生大量困惑。所以谢谢你能解释清楚。另外，我还看到过几个相关的问题，比如为什么不让那个.org域名由社区来运营呢？为什么不把它交给其他人管理，而非要自己独自把持呢？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Yeah, and the frame of that question is kind of interesting because it implies I'm the only person making WordPress which is obviously not true. If you look at the daily commits and activity and everything, it is run by the community. So it's hundreds of volunteers every day that are actually doing the day-to-day work and making the daily decisions and everything happens. So there has been a radical delegation. However, there's ultimately a hierarchy, and I'm the CEO, so I'm like the final final decision-maker. (01:02:24): And so I think what people advocate for around this governance point of view is like, okay, well, install a board on top of you that ultimately makes decisions for the product or things like that. And there are other open source projects that have this structure. None of them have been successful as WordPress. So I think your audience in particular, is great software ever created by committee or does it more often reflects a vision of a leader or something that can allow us to... and I think particularly WordPress not just remaining relevant but actually accelerating growth over huge technological shifts over the past two decades. (01:03:12): When we started there was dynamic web apps or DHTML or JavaScript wasn't really a thing, and then the social web and then iPhones and then all this sort of stuff that's changed over time, and we've surfed a lot of these technological changes which is very, very hard to do. Most products do not remain relevant over multiple generational changes like that, and that's been because sometimes we've had to make very unpopular decisions. Gutenberg is a huge part of why WordPress is relevant today, and it's actually an open source project we do. It's the block editor. It's actually bigger than WordPress because it's not just used on WordPress, it's used on every WordPress site, but also like Tumblr, other people. I would actually love if Squarespace or Wix adopted Gutenberg. It's meant to be like a really open source framework. (01:03:56): But anyway, if we had voted for whether we should do that or not, everyone would've voted against it or the majority would have. It was really a few core people of us in the community, Matias, myself, other core contributors, Ella, Andrew Ozz, that said, "Hey, this is the future and it's going to take 10 years to do and it's going to be a long bet. It's going to suck for the first three or four years, and so everyone's going to hate it in the beginning." (01:04:20): But then later with iteration, we've had I think now 200 releases of Gutenberg. We do sort of a very strict every two weeks release schedule since it started. It's going to get pretty good, and it's at that point now where it's actually getting pretty darn good. And the next phase of it, actually I'm so excited about, it's going to be collaboration. So all the real time co-editing like Google Docs and Notion has, it's coming out to this open source thing, and with the technological changes, we're actually able to do it peer-to-peer. So we don't need a centralized server. We can use WebRTC and other cool technologies. (01:04:49): I mean, anyway, I'm going sidelining, but I think that sort of more... and if you look at a lot of great companies, there's a board or whatever but ultimately there's an executive, and some of the most iconic companies of our generations are ones where the executive retains some majority of voting control or other things like that which I've been able to do with Automattic and with WordPress. And I definitely think about succession planning and everything like that, but if or when I'm gone I don't want to pass it to a committee. I want to pass it to someone else who can have a role similar to mine and really sort of try to be a steward. (01:05:34): There ultimately is a check and balance on that because, again, the community could leave. They could fork the software. People could change. And so you're "in charge" quote, unquote, but you're also at surface. So it's a lot more being like a mayor than a CEO and that you ultimately are accountable to the folks who are contributing and new users and everything like that. So I do feel like there is a balance there. Some of this as well is that there's some people who aren't part of leadership who feel like they should be. So if you look at the Yoast or Korean things, these are folks who actually don't have commit status. They haven't contributed WordPress over the years and serve our normal hierarchy of the meritocracy of how you get the ability to commit code or things like that. They're like, "Hey, I want to lead a release." That's cool, dude, but there's a process. We have different people lead releases over the years, but they kind of worked their way up to it.
turns.zh:
是啊，这个问题的框架挺有意思的，因为它暗示我是一个人独自开发WordPress的，但显然事实并非如此。如果你看看每日提交的代码、社区活动等数据，WordPress实际上是由数百名志愿者共同维护的。他们每天承担着日常工作、做出决策，整个项目得以运转。这是一个彻底的权力下放过程。不过最终还是存在层级结构，我作为CEO，承担着最终决策的责任。（01:02:24）：所以我认为围绕治理模式展开的讨论，比如成立一个委员会来做决策之类的，但这些项目从未像WordPress一样成功。我尤其想问听众们：软件是否能通过委员会治理成功，还是更需要领袖的愿景来推动？过去二十年间，WordPress不仅保持了相关性，还在技术变革中加速发展。这在其他开源项目中实属罕见。（01:03:12）：我们刚起步时，动态网页应用、DHTML、JavaScript都还不普及，接着是社交网络、iPhone等技术浪潮。我们成功驾驭了这些变革，多数产品难以在几代技术迭代中保持相关性。这背后有时需要做出不受欢迎的决策。Gutenberg是WordPress至今仍具竞争力的关键因素，它本质上是一个开源项目——块编辑器。它比WordPress本身更具影响力，除了WordPress站点，还应用于Tumblr等平台。我甚至希望Squarespace或Wix能采用Gutenberg。它本应成为一个开放的框架。（01:03:56）：但如果当初让大家投票决定是否采用Gutenberg，所有人都会反对，或者至少多数人反对。最终是社区中的核心成员——马蒂亚斯、我自己、其他核心贡献者埃拉、安德鲁·奥兹——坚持说："这是未来，需要十年时间打磨，前三年四年会很痛苦，刚开始大家都会讨厌它。"（01:04:20）：但经过迭代，我们已经发布了200个Gutenberg版本。自启动以来，我们严格遵循每两周一次的发布周期。现在它已经相当成熟，接下来将迎来协作阶段。谷歌文档和Notion等实时协作功能，将迁移到开源平台。借助WebRTC等技术，我们能实现端到端的协作，无需中央服务器。（01:04:49）：总之，我先不展开太多，但我认为大多数伟大公司都有董事会之类机构，但最终还是由高管掌控。我们这代人最具标志性的公司，其高管往往保留着多数投票权等控制权。我在Automattic和WordPress中成功实践了继任规划等机制。
是的，但如果我离开或者将来离开时，我不想把权力交给一个委员会。我希望把它交给一个能胜任类似我角色的人，让他们真正充当管理者的角色。（01:05:34）：最终还是存在制衡机制的，因为社区可能会离开，可能会分叉软件，人员可能会变动。所谓“掌管大局”，说白了不过是表面功夫。更像是市长而非CEO的角色，最终你要对贡献者、新用户等所有人负责。所以我确实觉得这里有种平衡。还有一些不参与领导层但自认为应该参与的人。比如Yoast和韩国团队的那些人，他们根本没有提交代码的权限。多年来他们没有为WordPress做出贡献，完全不符合贡献代码的资质标准。他们却说：“嘿，我想领导这次发布。”这想法挺好的，但流程摆在那儿。过去也有不同的人领导过发布，但他们都是一步步晋升上来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This makes so much sense to me. That's one of the themes of the podcast, just the power of a singular visionary and leader, founder mode as we've all heard is trending these days.
turns.zh: 这对我来说太有道理了。这正是播客的核心主题之一——一位独具远见的领导者所具有的力量，正如我们常说的“创始人模式”如今正大行其道。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: You made famous, yeah.
turns.zh: 你火了，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wouldn't say that it was. Yeah, Brian shared it, but then Paul Graham pointed afterwards and then I renamed the title of that episode Founder Mode to [inaudible 01:06:49]
turns.zh: 我不认为是这样。是的，布莱恩分享了这个观点，但后来保罗·格雷厄姆指出，随后我把那期节目的标题从“创始人模式”改名为[听不清 01:06:49]

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: I really want your [inaudible 01:06:50]
turns.zh: 我真的很想让你[听不清 01:06:50]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If I zoom out, what I'm sensing here is there's people that have this ideal of how something like this should run, but they've never actually worked at a place where a nonprofit board runs it, runs a thing, and have seen what that actually looks like. And so I think there's a big disconnect between the ideal in theory and how does great stuff get built.
turns.zh: 如果我退一步来看，我感觉这里存在一个很大的分歧。一方面，有些人对这类组织的运作方式有着理想化的设想，但他们从未在非营利性董事会管理的机构中工作过，亲眼见证过其运作模式。正因如此，我认为理论上的理想与实际构建伟大事物之间的脱节十分严重。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: And one of the things I think we've tried to demonstrate with WordPress is actually it's kind of like a open source side and a nonprofit side and a for-profit working in concert. And one of the things people don't necessarily appreciate as much about why WordPress has been so successful is because of Automattic and things like Akismet doing anti-spam or WordPress.com having a free version of WordPress that is introduced over a hundred million people to the software in a way that you could just sign up for free. You don't have to pay for hosting or download it yourself or things like that. (01:07:43): So that kind of for-profit, nonprofit, open source, working in concert I think is a really interesting model that we're starting to see a lot more companies do. It's actually very exciting to me that some of the things that were controversial when we started open source or distributed work are now the default for so many exciting new startups, and this whole ecosystems of really, really cool open source, like Cal.com for open source Calendly. There's so much cool stuff out there that actually there's a whole generation of younger entrepreneurs that I find very, very inspiring because they're also bringing modern design and web development and everything to open source which is very neat.
turns.zh: 我认为我们通过WordPress项目成功展示了开源、非营利组织和营利性公司协同运作的模式。人们往往没有充分意识到WordPress成功背后的原因——Automattic开发的反垃圾邮件插件Akismet，以及WordPress.com提供的免费版本，让数亿人得以免费体验这款软件，无需支付托管费用或自行下载。（01:07:43）：这种营利性、非营利性、开源三者协同运作的模式，着实令人振奋。如今，许多初创公司都遵循了我们早期开源或分布式工作的争议性理念，这实在令人欣喜。整个开源生态系统涌现出许多精彩项目，比如Cal.com这样的开源日历平台。新一代年轻创业者带来了现代设计、网络开发等元素注入开源领域，着实令人钦佩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I anticipate a blog post one day, "I told you so, guys." Open source, remote work, I imagine there's a few more things there. There's one other thing I want to address. I haven't seen you talk about this. It comes up a bunch. It's around, this is very the weeds, but I think it's really important to people, and there's something here for a lot of people, the way you guys forked Advanced Custom Fields. So I think what happened here is you guys forked an existing plugin, I think somebody else's plugin, and then kind of pushed people to this plugin versus the original plugin. What can you share there?
turns.zh: 我预料未来会有一篇博文写道："我就说吧，小伙子们。"开源、远程工作等领域，肯定还有更多值得探讨的议题。还有一件事我想谈谈。我没见你们提过，但这个话题经常被提及。这是个比较边缘的话题，但我认为对很多人很重要，比如你们如何分叉Advanced Custom Fields插件。当时你们分叉了一个现有插件，应该是别人的作品，然后引导用户使用新插件而非原版插件。能否谈谈当时的决策？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Yeah, this is very complex. So WordPress.org has kind of like a app store. After WP Engine started suing us, creating millions of dollars of legal fees and things, we blocked their access to WordPress.org. So this plugin they had, Advanced Custom Fields, wasn't able to be updated. At the same time a number of security issues were found in it, including some we reported, and so there had to be an update to it. So we're like, "Okay, we'll ship the update for you essentially." And then we were like, "Okay, I think we need to call it something different because it actually isn't theirs anymore." And they still offer Advanced Custom Fields on their own and people can download it from them, et cetera. So we made Secure Custom Fields which was originally under the same directory listing, so again, because we want all the users of it to get the security updates. This is controversial, and actually they actually got a preliminary injunction, so the judge said "Reverse this." So this has all been reversed by the way. (01:10:04): There now is a separate fork under separate listing of Secure Custom Fields which actually we have a team on it, developers, designers, and we're creating... just like WordPress was a fork, we've actually forged this. Actually WooCommerce was a forge. A lot of things are forks. So we forked it and now have a new name, new everything that we're doing a lot of product innovation and improving it. So there's a separate project now and separate directory listing for Secure Custom Fields. That's kind of fast-forward to today. They now have access to WordPress.org again. They have updated the plugin. Everything's back to how it was before, and there's now this separate thing called Secure Custom Fields that the WordPress project is officially supporting.
turns.zh: 是的，这事儿挺复杂的。WordPress.org其实就像一个应用商店。自从WP Engine开始起诉我们，导致我们产生了数百万美元的法律费用后，我们就封禁了他们访问WordPress.org的权限。结果他们之前开发的插件Advanced Custom Fields就无法更新了。同时，该插件被发现存在多项安全漏洞，包括我们曾报告过的一些问题，所以必须对其进行更新。我们当时就想：“好吧，我们可以替他们发布更新。”但后来我们又觉得：“或许应该给它换个新名字，因为它现在不属于他们了。” 于是我们把原名改成了Secure Custom Fields，仍保留在同一个目录下——这样所有用户都能获得安全更新。这引发了诸多争议，法官甚至下达了临时禁令，要求我们恢复原状。（01:10:04）：现在Secure Custom Fields在单独的目录下有独立分支，我们组建了团队，包括开发者和设计师，正在对其进行全面改进。实际上，WooCommerce本身也是一个分支项目。很多东西都是分支产物。所以我们分叉了这个项目，现在有了新名字、全新的一切，正在进行大量产品创新和改进。现在Secure Custom Fields有单独的项目和目录列表。事情发展到今天，他们现在又能访问WordPress.org了，插件也更新了，一切回归原状，而Secure Custom Fields这个独立项目现已获得WordPress项目的官方支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I'm hearing essentially you blocked WP Engine as a part of this, we're just going to simplify WordPress, reduce confusion. They're being bad actors in the space, so we're going to block them, and in that block, there's like a dependency where people couldn't do a thing that they needed to do. So you're like, "And the one that exists, there's a problem with it, so we're going to make that dependence... release a version that you can actually use and fix the security issues."
turns.zh: 所以我理解的核心是，你们封禁了WP Engine，目的是简化WordPress，减少混淆。他们在行业里属于不正派的角色，所以我们封禁了他们。封禁后，用户无法完成必要操作。于是你们就想：“现有版本有问题，我们要开发一个新版本，修复安全问题，让用户能正常使用。”

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: That was the intention. I think that there was a lot of perceptions around it that were different, but yeah, that was the goal.
turns.zh: 这就是初衷。我觉得外界对此有很多误解，但确实这就是我们的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay. Great. So maybe just the last question. We talked about just a lot of people see you with devil horns these days. They think you're doing bad things and they don't like the approach you're taking. You talked about there's this WP Engine spending a lot of money on PR and hiring this agency. I guess is there anything else that... why do you think so many people are looking at you as the bad guy? Is it mostly that you think... just where do you think it's coming from? Why are comments always so negative? And we talked a bit about it, but anything more there?
turns.zh: 好的，好的。很棒。最后可能还有个问题。我们注意到你最近经常戴恶魔角发饰，很多人觉得你做了很多坏事，不喜欢你的做法。你提到WP Engine花了很多钱请公关公司和代理机构。为什么这么多人把你视为反派？你觉得主要原因是什么？负面评论为何这么多？我们稍微讨论过，但还有更多想了解的？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: I don't know if I can say why. I do think one thing I've learned is that a lot of these things we've talked about are nuanced. So one essentially thing I've learned in this process is that it's hard to explain this stuff in 240 characters or the-
turns.zh: 我不知道该怎么解释。我确实意识到一个问题：很多我们讨论的复杂事务都需要细致入微地分析。在这个过程中，最深刻的体会就是用240个字符很难把事情解释清楚——

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: ... 40 characters. Some mediums do not lend themselves well to discussing this. And so I tried, but I'm participating less in Reddit or Twitter and trying to do more long form things like this, where you can actually have the context and things can't be taken out of context. Also, I think there's something where social networks sometimes are tuned to promote outrage. And it was very interesting. We ran a sentiment analysis recently. We were kind of looking at different social networks, analyzing all the comments, and we found, actually, that the negative, the sort of devil horn fraction on, what was it, like LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram was like 8%. It's actually pretty small. On Reddit, it was bigger, I forget the exact number, but on Twitter it was 52%. You're like, whoa, what's going on there? (01:12:53): And so there's something in the algorithm, and again, we can't see how the algorithm works or what the incentives are, but it can promote the most controversial things. I think that's not a novel perception. There's a lot of discussion around how social media might be creating more fragmentation in society, and I think this is just an example of that, where when you have networks, when people are getting the majority of the information from social networks, and those networks are not designed to provide nuance or balance, or even promote truth necessarily, misinformation can get spread far more than... What's the saying? Like a lie gets around the world seven times before truth has time to-
turns.zh: ……40个字符。有些平台不太适合讨论这个话题。所以我尝试过，但我现在在Reddit或Twitter上参与得越来越少，转而尝试做更长篇幅的内容，比如像这样的视频，这样你可以完整传达上下文，信息也不会被断章取义。此外，我觉得社交网络有时会刻意助长人们的愤怒情绪。这非常有趣。我们最近做了一次情感分析。我们研究了不同社交平台，分析了所有评论，结果发现，在LinkedIn、Facebook、Instagram等平台上，负面情绪（比如恶意评论）的比例约为8%，这个比例其实很低。而在Reddit上比例更高，我忘了具体数字，但在Twitter上则高达52%。你会惊讶地发现，这里面肯定有算法的因素，虽然我们看不到算法的具体运作机制，也不知道其背后的商业动机，但它确实会优先推送最具争议的内容。我觉得这并非新观点。现在有很多讨论，认为社交媒体可能正在加剧社会分裂，而这只是其中一个例子。当人们从社交平台获取大部分信息，而这些平台又不以提供细致的观点、平衡的视角或传播真相为己任时，虚假信息就会比真实信息传播得更广——正如那句谚语所说：谎言比真相传播得更快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Get out of bed.
turns.zh: 起床吧。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Get out of bed, yeah. There's been a lot of that. So there's actually been a lot of misinformation, untrue things that go viral, and then the untrue thing gets like 700,000 views, and the correction gets like 20,000 views. So there's been some of that happening. When mainstream media has covered this, it's actually been a lot better. So there's been some actually really good articles in some business publications and other things that sort of look at a more nuanced and balanced view. And I think the podcast have been pretty good, but definitely on Twitter, I think you can get a version of all of this that is both, I think, not entirely true and also pretty more negative.
turns.zh: 起床吧，对。这种情况挺常见的。所以确实有很多虚假信息、不实内容在社交媒体上疯传，然后虚假内容能获得70万次浏览量，而更正内容却只有2万次浏览量。这类情况屡见不鲜。当主流媒体报道这些问题时，报道得要好得多。所以有些商业刊物和其他媒体确实写过一些非常不错的文章，提供了更细致、更平衡的视角。我觉得播客也做得不错，但在Twitter上，你能看到的版本既不完全准确，又带有更负面的色彩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I imagine people are going to be like, "Lenny, you didn't ask him this thing. Here's the thing he said that I want to learn more about." I'm sure I missed some stuff, but from an outsider's perspective, this all make sense. There's a company, I don't think PE companies are bad innately, but their job is buy a company and make it run more efficiently, and then oftentimes sell it for more. So it makes sense that they buy a company, make it more efficient, cut some corners, don't put a lot of effort into making it awesome, even though I'm sure there's awesome people working in there, trying really hard to make it great. And basically what I'm feeling is they got to a point where this is hurting the ecosystem. They're feeling really dishonest with working with you, and there's a stalling technique. And so, makes sense to me why you just have to stand up and fight back. And it's hard, it's hard to do that. Is there anything else along this thread before we move on to a different topic, anything else you want to share before we close out this chapter?
turns.zh: 是啊。我能想象人们会说：“莱尼，你没问他这个问题啊。我想了解他说的那件事。”我肯定遗漏了些内容，但从旁观者的角度来看，这一切都说得通。有一家公司，我不认为私募股权公司天生就是坏的，但他们的职责是收购公司、提高效率，然后往往以更高的价格出售。所以他们收购公司、提高效率、削减成本、不在打造卓越产品上投入太多精力，这很正常——尽管我相信公司里肯定有很棒的人在努力让它变得出色。而我现在的感觉是，他们已经到了损害整个生态系统的地步。他们跟你合作时感觉很不诚实，这是一种拖延策略。所以在我看来，完全有必要挺身而出反击。这很难做到，真的很难。在我们转向下一个话题之前，这个话题还有什么其他内容吗？或者在结束这一章之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Well, if people have more questions, they can come to WordCamp Asia. We're going to do an open Q&A there. We do town halls in the WordPress.org Community. There's a Slack people can get on and ask questions. So there is kind of a lot of open ways to engage, and I'm definitely happy to do that. I'm probably not going to do it on Twitter as much, but when there's longer form opportunities to have a discussion here, particularly if it's more like real time, like this, I'm very happy to. (01:15:43): And that's why if you look at it, there's actually a big difference. WP Engine has not done any podcasts and no press. They don't respond to journalists, they don't talk about this. And I've done the opposite, where I'm really trying to be out there and engaged. And everyone's like, "Why don't you just let the lawyers do the talking?" And it's like, well, but we have community, and also I feel like we're in the right. So when you're in the wrong, you probably say only have the lawyers talk. When you're in the right, I think you should be out there and telling the story.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果大家还有更多问题，可以来参加亚太WordCamp大会。我们会在那里进行开放式的问答环节。在WordPress.org社区，我们也会举办市政厅会议。大家可以加入Slack平台提问。所以说，有很多公开的交流方式，我很乐意参与其中。不过我可能不会在Twitter上频繁发声，但当有更深入的讨论机会时，特别是像现在这种实时互动的机会，我会很乐意参与。（01:15:43）：这就是为什么，如果你仔细观察的话，其实会有很大的差别。WP Engine从未做过任何播客，也不接受媒体采访。他们不回应记者的问题，也不谈论这些事。而我做得恰恰相反，我一直积极参与其中。大家都问：“为什么不让律师来负责发言呢？”但我觉得，当你占据道德高地时，你就应该站出来讲述真相。而当你处于被动防守时，人们只会让律师来处理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember at the end of your WordCamp talk, you were like, "Any questions?" after this big controversial talk, and I'm curious how it felt. All the questions initially were nothing to do with this. It's what it felt like. You're just like, oh, they already had these questions. They didn't even know what you said maybe, and I bet you're just like, wait, did anyone hear what I just said? Did it feel like that?
turns.zh: 我记得在你的WordCamp演讲结束时，你问了句“还有什么问题吗？”在那场充满争议的演讲之后，大家的问题全然无关主题。那种感觉真是不一样。你会发现，人们甚至可能没听清你之前说了什么，我敢打赌你当时肯定在想：等等，有人听我说话了吗？那种感觉太明显了。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Well, also, that's really like a WordPress community event, so it's a lot of the core developers and things, so they have WordPress questions, so that is something.
turns.zh: 嗯，这毕竟是WordPress社区活动，所以来的人大多是核心开发者之类的，他们有WordPress相关的问题，这确实挺好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're like, hello.
turns.zh: 你好。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: I've now done hundreds and hundreds of these town halls and QAs, and I really enjoy it because you never know what's going to come up.
turns.zh: 我现在已经参加了数百场市政厅会议和问答环节，我非常享受这个过程，因为你永远不知道会碰到什么问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, okay. I want to talk about all the companies that you bought and will buy in the future. It's kind of like you're building a little Berkshire Hathaway. I think you've described it that way. It's kind of what it's feeling like. And Tumblr is really interesting. Until I started prepping for this, I didn't even know you guys own Tumblr. I haven't heard this story. Why did you guys buy Tumblr? What is going on with Tumblr? It was like a big deal back in the day. What is the current state of Tumblr? What is the story there?
turns.zh: 是的，好的。我想谈谈你收购的以及未来可能收购的公司。这有点像你在打造一个小型伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司。我记得你自己也这么形容过。确实有这种感觉。Tumblr真的很有趣。直到我开始为这次访谈做准备，我才知道你们收购了Tumblr。我之前从未听说过这个消息。你们为什么收购Tumblr？Tumblr现在情况如何？它曾是业界热议的话题。Tumblr目前的状态如何？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Oh, Tumblr is so interesting. At the time, I think it was one of our best competitors. They created this really amazing sort of hybrid of blogging and social networking. And if you kind of zoom back, a lot of things that are now standard on other social networks, even the ability to embed an image with a post, again, it was not supported originally on Twitter and other things. Remember they used to have, what was it, like tweet image, or you have to linked out to other things to post an image to Twitter. It wasn't native functionality, and Tumblr had these multiple post types. You could post a chat, an image. They were, I think, one of the first to support video, so they did a lot of, I think, product innovation under the leadership of David Karp, who's a really amazing entrepreneur and product leader. (01:17:54): Funny story, both David and I were at CNET at the same time. They had hired both of us.
turns.zh: 哦，Tumblr太有趣了。当时，我认为它是我们最强劲的竞争对手之一。他们创造了博客与社交网络的完美结合体。回顾过去，很多如今社交媒体上的标准功能，甚至是帖子中嵌入图片的功能，最初在Twitter等平台上都不支持。记得当时Twitter只允许在帖子中链接图片，不能直接嵌入。这些都不是原生功能，而Tumblr支持多种帖子类型。你可以发布聊天记录、图片。他们还是首批支持视频功能的平台之一，这都要归功于大卫·卡普（David Karp）的领导。他是一位非常出色的企业家和产品领袖。（01:17:54）：有趣的是，大卫和我曾同时在CNET工作，他们当时把我们俩都招了进来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an alumni group at CNET.
turns.zh: CNET的校友群真是了得。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: They could have kept both of us probably. But anyway, the Tumblr, I forget the year, but they sold, I think the same time that Instagram did, for a similar amount, $1.1 billion.
turns.zh: 他们本可以把我们俩都留住的。不过话说回来，Tumblr那事儿，我记不清具体年份了，但我记得他们是在和Instagram差不多同时被卖掉的，价格也差不多，11亿美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To you or to someone else?
turns.zh: 卖给你们还是卖给别人了？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Instagram bought by Facebook, obviously.
turns.zh: 显然是被Facebook收购了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, right. Tumblr.
turns.zh: 对，对。Tumblr。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: And Tumblr bought by Yahoo.
turns.zh: 然后Tumblr被雅虎收购了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Who was at the time, again, Yahoo, we don't think about it now, but I feel a little old. But at the time, Yahoo was one of the internet giants and had recently Marissa Mayer, who was one of the big early people at Google, I think part of creating the API program and everything like that, was the CEO of Yahoo. This was, I think, one of her first big acquisitions. (01:18:46): Now subsequently, obviously ,we know how Instagram went. I think people were like, "I can't believe you bought this for a billion dollars." And obviously now it's worth hundreds of billions. So that's had a really good trajectory. At Yahoo, I think things became more challenged. So again, this is a little bit of history, but Yahoo then had this thing where they owned part of Alibaba, which then became more valuable than the rest of the company. They had activist investors. I think they had some CEO switches. I think Marissa Mayer leaves or gets fired at some point. There's all this turnover, and I think Tumblr really languished under their ownership. And from what I can understand, the team was actually held back a lot from things they wanted to launch or ways they wanted to iterate. Then Yahoo merges with AOL, which is another kind of early internet thing. That goes for a little while. So again, then Tumblr's just kind of stuck underneath this stuff.
turns.zh: 当时雅虎还是谁来着？现在我们都不太记得了，但我感觉自己有点老了。不过当时雅虎可是互联网巨头之一，而且当时刚任命了玛丽莎·梅耶尔。她是谷歌早期的重要人物之一，参与了API项目等开发，现在雅虎CEO。她收购Tumblr应该算是她执掌雅虎后的首笔大交易。（01:18:46）：之后大家都知道Instagram的发展了。当时人们都惊呼“难以置信你们花10亿美元买了这个”。而现在Instagram市值已经数百亿美元了。发展轨迹真是惊人。雅虎方面则陷入了困境。当时雅虎持有阿里巴巴的部分股权，后来阿里巴巴的价值远超雅虎其他资产，还有激进投资者介入，CEO更迭，玛丽莎·梅耶尔离职或被解雇，管理层频繁变动，而Tumblr在雅虎旗下也发展缓慢。据我了解，雅虎团队被严格限制，无法推进许多创新计划。后来雅虎与AOL合并，AOL也是早期互联网巨头，但合并后的业务也未能成功。最终Tumblr被Verizon收购。时间快进到2019年，Verizon想摆脱Tumblr，于是挂牌出售，收到了多个竞标，最终Automattic以极低价格收购。据报道，我们只花了300万美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tumbling along.
turns.zh: 真是便宜啊。300万。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Tumbling along. And then that gets bought by Verizon. So fast-forward to 2019. Verizon wants to get rid of Tumblr. And so they're kind of putting it up for sale and had a number of bidders. Automattic ended up buying it for a de minimis amount. I think it's been reported we bought it for $3 million.
turns.zh: 真是便宜啊。然后又被Verizon收购。快进到2019年。Verizon想摆脱Tumblr，于是挂牌出售，收到了多个竞标，最终Automattic以极低价格收购。据报道，我们只花了300万美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a deal. 3 million.
turns.zh: 真划算。300万。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: But obviously, that represented a lot of value destruction over the years. Tumblr had had some tough times. They actually were banned from the App Store at one point for not moderating things well enough and having maybe a little too much porn. Obviously, Twitter [inaudible 01:20:31] porn. They maybe were a little too out there with it, and we're doing a good job filtering it and keeping away from App Store reviewers or whatever. And so Verizon, to their credit though, there were people bidding more. Actually I think a porn company was bidding on Tumblr that would've paid a lot more money. They really were looking for an acquirer that they felt like would be a good steward. From my point of view, I had such incredible respect for Tumblr as a product. And the community, still, despite all of this sort of stuff that had happened, I think at that point still was like, I forget the exact number, but call it 15, 20 million monthly active users. (01:21:14): So really, sort of active core. And one of the things that's so fascinating is over half of that user base was under the age of 25. And actually had a huge, I think, it was like 25 or 30% LGBT+. I think a very unique place on the internet, where people could have a social network where they could be anonymous, they could put on different identities, they could be someplace their parents weren't, like Facebook or Instagram, really still could take a special spot. So we ended up buying it. Now, people are like, "Oh, you bought it for $3 million." But we bought it sort of taking on all liabilities, including, I think they were under investigation by the FTC, there were lawsuits. There was all this sort of stuff. So it was free like a puppy, not free like-
turns.zh: 显然，这些年来Tumblr的价值被严重削弱了。它曾经历过一段艰难时期。事实上，该平台曾因未能有效监管内容且色情内容泛滥而被苹果应用商店下架。推特（Twitter）也曾因类似问题被禁（未录音部分01:20:31），色情内容问题处理得有些过火。不过值得称赞的是，Verizon的竞标方出价更高。据我所知，甚至有一家色情公司愿意出更高价收购Tumblr，他们显然在寻找一个能妥善管理平台的买家。就我个人而言，我对Tumblr作为产品深怀敬意。即便经历了种种风波，其社区活跃用户数量依然可观——当时月活跃用户约1500万至2000万（01:21:14），其中超过半数用户年龄在25岁以下。LGBT+群体占比更是高达25%至30%。这是一个独特的网络空间，用户可以匿名社交、隐藏真实身份，远离父母的监管，比如Facebook或Instagram这样的平台根本无法复制这种独特体验。最终我们收购了Tumblr。如今人们会说“你们只花了300万美元买下它”。但实际上，我们接手时承担了所有债务，包括FTC的调查、法律诉讼等诸多风险。这次收购就像收养一只小狗，绝非免费——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Free like beer.
turns.zh: 而是像买啤酒——

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Had a pretty big team, I think 185 people. We were taking a lot of burners, burning a ton of cash, and that was 2019. And so, it's been, I think, a humbling experience running a social network. It was very, very different from all the other products that we've done. And I think there's some incredible things about Tumblr and that I'm still very excited about. So where WordPress has primarily a desktop and web user base, Tumblr is obviously like 85% app-based, has a younger demographic. And so part of the vision that now we're executing on is actually we wanted to create a path for people using Tumblr to actually it being powered by WordPress on the back end. So Tumblr users could unlock themes, customization, plugins, et cetera. Actually, we're in the process right now of migrating the half a billion Tumblr sites to WordPress, probably one of the largest data migrations-
turns.zh: 当时我们组建了185人的团队，烧钱如流水，那还是2019年的事。运营社交网络的挑战超乎想象，与我们之前的产品完全不同。Tumblr仍有许多亮点，我至今仍对它充满热情。与WordPress主要面向桌面和网页用户不同，Tumblr85%的用户通过应用访问，用户群体更年轻。我们目前的愿景是让Tumblr用户在后台使用WordPress的技术支持，解锁主题、自定义功能、插件等。目前我们正将5亿个Tumblr站点迁移至WordPress，这可能是史上最大规模的数据迁移之一——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense.
turns.zh: 这说得通。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: ... that's happened in a while. So we're kind of trying to do this in a way that's invisible to users on the front end, so changing at the back end while maintaining the APIs and the interface and everything. So it's a fun engineering project. I kind of posted this kind of call to arms, got a lot of fun people applying for Automattic, and we hired a lot of great folks around this sort of audacious project, this big hairy audacious goal. And so that's where it's at now. I've sort of ran it personally for a few years while we're doing turnarounds, but there's a great team there, but still challenged, still not profitable, so we're still subsidizing it from the rest of Automattic's businesses. Fortunately, the rest of our business have done really well, so we were able to do that, but I definitely want to get to a place where it's sustainable. (01:23:46): And one of the things we're also experimenting with is can Tumblr have not just an advertising-driven model? I think ultimately the incentives of advertising social networks can lead to the kind of dynamics that you see on the more negative side of Twitter, Instagram, Facebook, et cetera. And so really trying to create a subscription model or a sort of first-party user-driven advertising, where you promote your blog posts or something like that, or you promote a WooCommerce product or something, where it's not a third-party ad ecosystem, which I think has a lot of weird code and malware and lots of stuff I don't love.
turns.zh:
嗯，确实有段时间没发生这种事了。所以我们正试图以一种用户在前端看不出来的方式来推进这项工作，后端进行调整，同时保持API、界面等一切不变。这真是个有趣的工程项目。我发了一篇类似“号召令”的帖子，吸引了不少有才华的人申请加入Automattic，我们为这个雄心勃勃的项目招募了许多优秀人才。这就是目前的进展。在过渡阶段，我亲自负责了几年，但现在已经组建了一支强大的团队。不过业务仍不盈利，所以我们仍在从Automattic的其他业务中抽取资金补贴。幸运的是，其他业务发展得非常好，才得以维持这一局面。但我确实希望能让Tumblr实现可持续发展。

（01:23:46）：我们还在尝试的一个方向是，Tumblr能否不局限于广告驱动模式？我认为，最终广告驱动的社交媒体平台可能会导致类似推特、Instagram、脸书等平台负面效应的出现。因此，我们正努力创建订阅模式或用户主导的广告体系，比如推广博客文章、WooCommerce产品等，而非依赖第三方广告生态系统——那种充斥着恶意代码和各种问题的生态环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, sounds like a lot you took on with this acquisition, and I love that you said you ran it initially. So this is a good segue to maybe my last question. I'm curious where this goes. Just how do you... Well, let me zoom out. There's a lot of people these days that are excited about roll of businesses. I'm going to buy a bunch of companies, make them better, make them awesome, save money, and then just keep building this holding company sort of thing. You guys are doing that, and it's working well. What do you look for? How do you decide a company's right for Automattic? What are the factors that are like, we should buy this, we can turn this around and turn it into a big success?
turns.zh: 哇，收购Tumblr后你们承担了不少挑战，我很欣赏你最初亲自操盘的做法。这让我能顺势提问我的最后一个问题。我很好奇Tumblr的未来走向。你们是如何运营的？又如何判断一家公司是否适合Automattic？哪些因素决定了我们应该收购它、扭转局面并将其打造成成功案例？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: I don't know if I would do another turnaround like Tumblr again, or at least not for many, many years. It's definitely a different thing. The vast majority of things we acquire, it's simply something that's done well, and we want to accelerate it, or sometimes acqui-hires, where we're plugging it into one of our existing projects, or we're taking the team and putting them on something we're already doing. So it's a really talented team. Tumblr, I think we ended up ultimately replacing 85, 90% of the team as well. So that's just very different. So I do think there are different ways of doing it, but if you look at our other acquisitions like Day One, et cetera, founder's still here, many years later, we're accelerating stuff like that. We brought it to Android, we're bringing it to it to web. It's more of taking something good and making it better. And probably our best example there is WooCommerce, which was a small company, I think 35, 40 people, based out of South Africa, and has obviously grown to... Again, I said Automattic makes about half a billion dollars a year now, and WooCommerce is a majority of that.
turns.zh: 我不确定自己是否会再经历像Tumblr这样的转型，至少未来很长一段时间都不会了。那确实是完全不同的情况。我们收购的大多数公司都表现出色，我们希望加速其发展，有时会进行收购整合，将其融入现有项目，或是让团队转向我们正在推进的方向。Tumblr的团队规模很大，甚至换掉了85%至90%的原班人马。这完全不同。所以我认为确实有不同的运作方式，但看看我们其他的收购案例，比如Day One等公司，创始人多年后仍在公司，我们正在加速其发展。我们将Day One引入安卓平台，推向网页端。更多的是在现有基础上优化提升。WooCommerce就是最典型的例子。这家公司最初只有35、40名员工，总部位于南非，如今显然已发展壮大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, actually, you haven't shared the revenue number. I know it's public. Just give people a sense of Automattic's revenue. Can you just share those numbers? Because I think it might blow people's minds.
turns.zh: 说到这儿，其实你还没透露过营收数据。我知道这信息是公开的。能不能给听众讲讲Automattic的营收情况？因为我觉得这数字可能会让大家大吃一惊。

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Yeah, I think we say publicly it's about a half a billion dollars in sort of ARR revenue right now.
turns.zh: 是的，我想我们公开的信息是，目前的年度经常性收入（ARR）约为5亿美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible. Okay. I have a question for you. It's kind of a hot seat question. As you talked, I wonder, I feel like people are thinking of this. So you've been talking about PE companies being often bad. You're buying Tumblr. You've talked about laying off a bunch of people, turning it all around. How's that different from a PE company, Matt?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。好的，我有个尖锐的问题。听你讲话的时候，我感觉大家都在思考这个问题。你一直在说私募股权公司往往不善于经营，而你们收购了Tumblr，还裁减了大量员工，成功扭转了局面。这和私募股权公司有何不同，马特？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Yeah, and I agree with you that just because it's private equity doesn't mean it's bad. And also, something people say is like, "Hey, wait, don't you have private equity investors as well at Automattic?" And we do. Now, they own usually a small percentage, sometimes under 1%, and they don't have control of the company. So I think there's a distinguish. Is it a minority investment or a control investment? And with WP Engine, Silver Lake controls the company. And when they control the company, I think there's a spectrum of actions. Obviously, being more efficient is great, and we should all strive for that. And I think every business does, whether it's private equity or our business or things that are founder controlled. You always want to be more efficient. Now, there's some spectrum there where you over-optimize, or you could have dark patterns. Right now on WP Engine, it's very difficult to cancel your accounts. Actually, I think as of today, 45,000 sites have left, so they're, I think, down to 600. Yeah, well, because their customers have realized like, "Hey, this isn't WordPress, this isn't..." or, "They're suing the guy who started WordPress, so maybe we should not support this commercially." So we have the site wordpressenginetracker.com that sort of shows in real time the sites that are leaving. It's kind of an exciting thing to see that number tick up. Actually, maybe a good example as well, even though there's a lot of negativity, you actually look at how people are voting with their wallets. They're leaving. (01:28:07): So I think you have to judge as well, just look at the track record. So one of the things I'm very proud of with Automattic is we are an acquirer of first resort, and we have founders that have sold to us. Paul Mayne at Day One is a great example that didn't need to sell. They're wildly profitable, could have run it himself for a long, long time, but people choose to join because they feel like we'll be good stewards of it in the future, and ultimately just have to look at the track record. (01:28:36): So I think don't judge it by what it's called, judge it by the actions over time. And I hope to continue building that reputation for a place that's a good steward of communities and software and everything else for many years to come.
turns.zh: 是的，我同意你的观点，私募股权并不意味着糟糕。还有人会问：“嘿，等等，Automattic不是也有私募股权投资者吗？”确实有。但他们通常只持有很小的股份，往往不足1%，而且无法控制公司。所以这有本质区别。是少数股权投资还是控制性投资？拿WP Engine来说，Silver Lake控制了公司。当私募股权公司控制公司时，行为往往存在灰色地带。显然，提高效率是好的，我们都应该为此努力。无论是私募股权公司、我们自己的业务，还是创始人控制的公司，每个企业都希望提高效率。但这里有过度优化和暗藏陷阱的风险。比如现在WP Engine很难注销账户。实际上，截至今天，已有4.5万个网站离开平台，剩下约600个。原因是用户意识到：“嘿，这不是WordPress，这不是……” 或者，“他们正在起诉WordPress的创始人，所以我们或许不该支持这项商业服务。”所以我们建立了网站wordpressenginetracker.com，实时显示离平台的网站数量。看到这个数字不断攀升真是令人兴奋。即便负面声音很多，但人们用实际行动投票。（01:28:07）所以评判时要看实际表现。我对Automattic最自豪的一点是，我们是首选收购方，许多创始人都愿意把公司卖给我们。Day One的保罗·梅恩就是典范，他本不必出售公司。他们利润丰厚，本可以自己经营很久，但人们选择加入，因为相信我们未来会妥善管理公司，最终还是要看实际表现。（01:28:36）所以别看标签，看行动。希望未来多年，我们能继续树立良好声誉，成为社区、软件等领域的优秀管理者。

So very, very excited about that relaunch. So I encourage people to, you check out the beta now, go to beeper.com/beta to get the new version, and we're going to relaunch that later in the year. (01:29:50): So yeah, I'm very excited about that. It's kind of fun to be working on something that's at the stage where WordPress was in 2003, 2004. So WordPress is quite mature at this point. WooCommerce is kind of where WordPress was in 2010. And then the Beeper stuff, the messaging stuff is where we were in 2003. So one thing that keeps me excited is working at different stages of this.
turns.zh: 是的，关注我吧。我在Tumblr、Twitter、Instagram等平台上的账号都是"photomatt"，拼写是P-H-O-T-M-A-T-T。我主要分享其他方面的内容，比如人工智能、开源项目，还有一些WordPress相关的内容。我还有个毕生使命，就是让出版和商业变得民主化。去年我们新增了一个功能——即时通讯，目前还在测试阶段，但几个月后就会正式上线产品"Beeper"，它能整合你所有的Telegram、Instagram私信、Signal等消息平台，统一管理所有对话。用户还能进行很多酷炫的操作，特别是结合本地AI的搜索功能，这让我特别兴奋。（01:29:50）所以我鼓励大家现在就去体验测试版，访问beeper.com/beta获取最新版本，今年晚些时候我们会正式发布。（01:31:25）能参与不同阶段的产品开发真的很棒。

turns.zh: 这让我明白，为什么你要关注伯克希尔哈撒韦这样的公司，就是要在早期阶段保持活力，而不只是优化现有事物。顺便说一下，Beeper的域名很棒。Photomatt这个名字有什么故事吗？我猜你应该和摄影有关吧？

turns.speaker: Matt Mullenweg
turns.en: Yeah, it's a little bit of a pun. So a fotomatt is also, F-O-T-O-M-A-T-T, is a place that you would go to develop your photos back when you would have film and develop things. So originally my username was Saxmatt because I played the saxophone. Sometimes people mishear that. And also, I started traveling so much. There's been years I do like 400,000 miles of air travel, because I go around the world to go to WordPress events and meet the community. And as a distributed company, we do lots of meetups. And so, it became hard to carry my saxophone around. So my method of artistic expression became photography, and that's actually kind of how WordPress started, was actually originally a site where I could share my photos before Flickr, before Facebook and everything like that, sort of use this gallery software, actually open source gallery software, PHP software, to sort of share all the photos I was taking. (01:31:25): And actually now on my website, I think I have over 38,000 photos I posted. And yeah, it's still one of the things I really love. So it's also a username that was available everywhere, and I still do it. So I'm actually going to the Maha Kumbh Mela, the big 300-million-person gathering at the Ganges River in a few weeks. turns.zh: 是的，这是个双关语。Fotomatt也是“F-O-T-O-M-A-T-T”，指的是冲洗胶片照片的地方。最初我的用户名是Saxmatt，因为我会萨克斯风，有时人们会听错。后来我开始频繁旅行，有些年份飞行里程高达40万英里，因为我要参加WordPress活动、与社区互动。作为分布式公司，我们常举办聚会，但带着萨克斯风太不方便了。于是摄影成了我的艺术表达方式，而WordPress最初也是这样——在Flickr和Facebook出现前，我用开源的PHP图库软件分享照片。（01:31:25）现在我的网站上应该有超过38,000张照片。这依然是我热爱的事。用户名在各平台都可用，我至今还在用。几周后我要去恒河岸边参加大壶节，这场每12年一次、吸引3亿人参加的盛会。我既期待亲身感受，又想好好拍照。
